scenes.title: The easiest list to sort
scenes.narration: Sorting a whole list at once feels hard, because every number competes with every other number.

steps.say: Here are eight numbers in no order at all.
But what is the easiest list in the world to sort? A list with just one item.
Is forty two sorted? Yes. A single item is always in order.
Merge sort uses that. It breaks the list down until every piece is one item, then stitches the pieces back together in order.

scenes.title: Split in half, again and again

steps.say: Find the middle, and cut the list in two.
Cut each half in two again.
And again, until every piece is a single item. That is where the splitting stops.
Notice that no number has changed places yet. We have only pulled them apart.

scenes.title: Merging single items into pairs
scenes.narration: Step two is to merge. Start with the first two single items.

steps.say: Compare fifty one and thirteen. Thirteen is smaller.
So thirteen goes first.
Then fifty one. That pair is sorted.
Same for eighty nine and four. Four is smaller.
So four goes first, then eighty nine.

scenes.title: Merging two sorted pairs
scenes.narration: Now merge the two sorted pairs. Both are already in order, so we only ever look at the front of each one.

steps.say: Compare thirteen and four. Four is smaller.
So four takes the first spot, and the right pair moves on to eighty nine.
Compare thirteen and eighty nine. Thirteen wins.
Thirteen takes the next spot, and the left pair moves on to fifty one.
Fifty one against eighty nine. Fifty one wins.
Now the left pair is used up.
So the leftover eighty nine just copies over. It is like two sorted decks of cards feeding one sorted pile.

scenes.title: Every level moves all eight once
scenes.narration: The same zipper runs at every level, until the whole list is back together.

steps.say: Merging into pairs moves all eight numbers once.
Merging pairs into fours moves all eight again.
And the last merge moves all eight one more time. The list is sorted.
Halving eight items takes three levels, which is log two of eight.
Each level does about n work. So the total is n times log n.

scenes.narration: Compare that with a simple sort that checks every pair, which takes about n squared steps.

steps.say: n squared shoots up. At a hundred twenty eight items it is over sixteen thousand.
n log n climbs gently, to under nine hundred.
That is about ninety five percent less work. And merge sort gets this every time. Unlike quicksort, it has no bad pivot days.
